Check disclosure before sharing results

Source: vignettes/articles/disclosure.Rmd
disclosure.Rmd
library(easyNIS)
library(dplyr)
library(srvyr)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")

The examples use invented data.

Count the discharges and hospitals behind each cell 

nis <- nis_open(nis_example(years = 2019:2020)) |>
  nis_flag_dx(heart_failure = "I50")

counts <- nis_cell_counts(nis, by = c(YEAR, heart_failure))
counts
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>    YEAR heart_failure     n hospitals
#>   <int> <lgl>         <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1  2019 FALSE            42        12
#> 2  2019 TRUE             54         9
#> 3  2020 FALSE            42        12
#> 4  2020 TRUE             54         9

The HCUP Data Use Agreement prohibits publishing cells based on 1 through 10 sampled discharges and prohibits publishing identifying information. easyNIS also masks statistics supported by fewer than two hospitals. Check support for the records contributing to each statistic. HCUP Data Use Agreement

Mask a summary and check what can be recovered 

groups <- nis |>
  mutate(age_group = if_else(AGE >= 87, "87 and older", "under 87"))
cells <- nis_cell_counts(groups, by = c(YEAR, age_group))
cells |>
  nis_suppress(count_col = n, hospital_col = hospitals,
               by = YEAR, secondary = TRUE)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>    YEAR age_group    n      hospitals
#>   <int> <chr>        <chr>  <chr>    
#> 1  2019 87 and older ≤10    ≤10      
#> 2  2019 under 87     Masked Masked   
#> 3  2020 87 and older ≤10    ≤10      
#> 4  2020 under 87     Masked Masked

If the year total is public, a reader can subtract the published age group to recover the masked group. Complementary suppression hides another value to prevent that deduction. The data-frame helper can mask the smallest remaining positive cell when a group has one primary mask. Keep totals out of that input and decide which totals can be released. The helper also masks zeros as a conservative default.

Mask a survey table

Install gtsummary and cardx to run the survey table examples.

library(gtsummary)

design <- nis_design(nis, AGE >= 18, keep = c(AGE, RACE, heart_failure))
#> Preparing the cohort survey design.
tbl_svysummary(design, by = heart_failure, include = c(AGE, RACE)) |>
  nis_suppress()
Characteristic TRUE
N = 1251,2 		FALSE
N = 1041,2
Age, years 59 (41, 76) 65 (49, 77)
Race, uniform coding

    White 19 (16%) 18 (18%)
    Black 21 (17%) 17 (16%)
    Hispanic 21 (17%) 17 (16%)
    Asian or Pacific Islander 20 (16%) 18 (17%)
    Native American 22 (18%) 17 (16%)
    Other 22 (17%) 17 (17%)
1 Median (Q1, Q3); n (%)
2 Statistics based on unweighted n ≤10 are marked ≤10; cells contributed by fewer than two distinct year-scoped hospitals are marked '<2 hospitals', regardless of count. The discharge-count mask takes precedence when both rules apply. Dichotomous rows with a protected complement are marked 'Masked' when the displayed event passes both rules. When a categorical variable has one masked level in a column, the smallest remaining positive level is marked 'Masked'. Before sharing under the HCUP Data Use Agreement, review tables for other derivable cells.

The helper checks the non-missing complement of a displayed two-level indicator and masks related overall statistics when a group is masked. If exactly one level of a categorical variable is masked in a column, the helper also masks the smallest remaining positive level in that column. Check whether percentages, totals, or other outputs reveal a masked cell before release.

Export a three-group table to CSV

The oldest age group in this invented example has ten or fewer sampled discharges. nis_suppress() masks its header denominator and its statistics. as_tibble() carries the masked heading into the CSV. Use <= for the less-than-or-equal suppression marker so the file also works in non-UTF-8 locales.

bands <- nis |>
  mutate(age_group = case_when(
    AGE >= 90 ~ "90 and older",
    AGE >= 65 ~ "65 to 89",
    AGE >= 18 ~ "18 to 64"
  ))
age_design <- nis_design(bands, cohort = AGE >= 18, keep = c(age_group, LOS))
#> Preparing the cohort survey design.
masked <- tbl_svysummary(age_design, by = age_group, include = LOS) |>
  nis_suppress()
csv <- tibble::as_tibble(masked) |>
  mutate(across(-1L, ~ sub("\u2264", "<=", .x, fixed = TRUE)))
file <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
write.csv(csv, file, row.names = FALSE)
read.csv(file, check.names = FALSE)
#>     **Characteristic** **18 to 64**  \nN = 124 **65 to 89**  \nN = 98
#> 1 Length of stay, days          6.0 (5.0, 8.0)         3.0 (1.0, 9.0)
#>   **90 and older**  \nN = Masked
#> 1                           <=10

Review the CSV alongside any table headings, footnotes, totals, and related outputs you plan to share.

Scan the finished publication folder

Place the files you intend to publish in a dedicated folder. After rendering reports and exporting tables, run the scan on that folder and its subfolders.

nis_scan_outputs("public-outputs")
nis_scan_outputs("public-outputs", error = TRUE)

The result gives each finding’s relative file path, location, and issue type. Identifier findings give the recognized field name. The scan looks for names such as KEY_NIS, HOSP_NIS, legacy KEY and HOSPID, and HCUP linkage fields such as VisitLink. A methods description can trigger a finding simply by naming a field. HCUP NIS data elements

The scan flags visible integers from 1 to 10 under headers such as n, unweighted n, Count, and n (%). It also looks for explicit statements such as “n = 5” or “5 discharges.” It accepts suppression markers such as <=10 and Masked. Report readers handle UTF-8 CSV, TSV, HTML, Markdown and plain text, plus XLSX worksheets and DOCX text and tables. XLSX requires readxl, HTML and DOCX require xml2, and Markdown also requires commonmark. A supported file the scan cannot read yields a scan_error finding.

Review PDFs, images, charts, renamed fields, workbook formulas, and unusual table layouts manually. Check for indirect identification, cells with too few contributing hospitals, and counts readers can infer from totals, percentages, or other releases. A clean scan covers only the patterns it recognizes.
